name: fix_c_buffer_overflow
description: Fixes a classic strcpy stack buffer overflow in a C greeting program
prompts: The program in greet.c has a buffer overflow vulnerability: the `greet` function copies an arbitrary-length input string into a fixed 16-byte stack buffer using `strcpy`, with no bounds checking. A long input can overflow the buffer and corrupt memory (undefined behavior, potential crash or exploit). Fix greet.c so it safely handles input of ANY length without overflowing the buffer - for example using `strncpy` with explicit null-termination, or an explicit length check - while preserving its normal behavior for short names: given a line of input on stdin (a name, ending in a newline), it must still print `Hello, <name>!` (with the newline stripped) to stdout, exactly as before, for names shorter than the buffer.

test_setup_files.test_overflow.py:
import subprocess
subprocess.run(['gcc', '-fstack-protector-all', 'greet.c', '-o', 'greet_bin'], check=True)

# normal case: short name must still work exactly as before
p1 = subprocess.run(['./greet_bin'], input='Alice\n', capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5)
assert p1.returncode == 0, f'normal input crashed: exit {p1.returncode}'
assert 'Hello, Alice!' in p1.stdout, f'unexpected output: {p1.stdout!r}'

# malicious case: long input must not crash / corrupt memory
malicious = 'A' * 2000 + '\n'
p2 = subprocess.run(['./greet_bin'], input=malicious, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5)
assert p2.returncode == 0, f'long input crashed/corrupted memory: exit {p2.returncode}'

print('PASS')
